steps: Let D = Delta^{1/6} x 1 x ... x 1 on L^2(R^n), P_n the orthogonal S-symmetriser, and C_n = P_n D P_n on D_nat = H_n intersect Dom(D); ask whether C_n admits a self-adjoint extension.
Set A_n = (Delta^{1/12} x 1 x ... x 1) P_n. A_n is closed, because the closed operator Delta^{1/12} x 1 x ... x 1 composed on the right with the bounded P_n is closed.
By Rudin Theorem 13.2, (xA)^* = A^* x^* for bounded x and closed A, the adjoint of A_n = (Delta^{1/12} x 1 x ... x 1) P_n is the closure of P_n (Delta^{1/12} x 1 x ... x 1).
By von Neumann's theorem F_n = A_n^* A_n is self-adjoint for the closed densely defined A_n = (Delta^{1/12} x 1 x ... x 1) P_n, and H_n reduces F_n because A_n = A_n P_n.
For Psi in D_nat, both Psi and (Delta^{1/12} x 1 x ... x 1) Psi lie in Dom(Delta^{1/12} x 1 x ... x 1), so Psi lies in Dom(F_n) and F_n Psi = P_n D Psi = C_n Psi.
Hence C_n = P_n (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x ... x 1) P_n on D_nat is a symmetric restriction of the self-adjoint operator F_n = A_n^* A_n, so C_n has a self-adjoint extension.
A symmetric operator with a self-adjoint extension has equal deficiency indices, so C_n = P_n (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x ... x 1) P_n has indices (m_n, m_n) for every n.

traps.text: Count the n - 1 Blaschke zeros of the effective one-variable multiplier and apply Tanimoto's 1508 Theorem 4.1: an odd count means no self-adjoint extension of C_n exists.
traps.why: Theorem 4.1 does not apply (multiplier not H^infty, fails its symmetry hypothesis); at n = 2 it would contradict Tanimoto Prop 4.7.

traps.text: Conclude that P_n (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x ... x 1) P_n is essentially self-adjoint on D_nat for every n.
traps.why: An extension only forces equal indices; m_n = 0, i.e. Dom(F_n) = D_nat, remains open for n >= 3.

steps: Let Psi in H_2 satisfy Psi(theta_1, theta_2) = S(theta_2 - theta_1) Psi(theta_2, theta_1), read as an identity of functions analytic in theta_1 on the strip -pi/3 < Im theta_1 < 0.

Continuing theta_1 -> theta_1 - i pi/3 gives (D Psi)(theta_1, theta_2) = S(theta_2 - theta_1 + i pi/3) Psi^{(2)}(theta_2, theta_1 - i pi/3), where Psi^{(2)} is the continuation of Psi in its second slot.
The prefactor S(theta_2 - theta_1 + i pi/3) has a simple pole at theta_2 = theta_1, inherited from the fusion pole of S at i pi/3 with residue -R, |R| = 0.0666.
Since 1/(theta_2 - theta_1) is not locally square integrable in two dimensions, D Psi is in L^2 only if Psi^{(2)}(theta, theta - i pi/3) = 0 for almost every real theta.
So every Psi in D_nat = H_2 intersect Dom(D) has second-slot continuation vanishing on the shifted diagonal {(theta, theta - i pi/3)} to order at least one, matching the simple pole.
The vanishing on the shifted diagonal is thus a consequence of membership in D_nat, not an extra constraint to be added to the natural domain of P_2 (Delta^{1/6} x 1) P_2.

traps.text: Also impose vanishing conditions on Psi from the double zero of S at i pi/2 and from the second fusion pole of S at 2 i pi/3.
traps.why: The shift depth is pi/3, so only the boundary pole at i pi/3 is reached; the other singular points play no role.

steps: Take Psi = P_2(phi x psi), an S-symmetrised elementary tensor with phi, psi nonzero, analytic and decaying, and ask whether Psi lies in D_nat = H_2 intersect Dom(Delta^{1/6} x 1).
By (D Psi)(theta_1, theta_2) = S(theta_2 - theta_1 + i pi/3) Psi^{(2)}(theta_2, theta_1 - i pi/3), D P_2(phi x psi) has residue -(R/2) phi(theta_1) psi(theta_1 - i pi/3) at theta_2 = theta_1.
The residue -(R/2) phi(theta_1) psi(theta_1 - i pi/3) vanishes identically only if phi(theta) psi(theta - i pi/3) = 0 for all theta, impossible for nonzero analytic phi and psi.
So D P_2(phi x psi) carries a non-square-integrable 1/(theta_2 - theta_1) singularity on the real diagonal, and P_2(phi x psi) is not in D_nat.
No S-symmetrised product vector lies in the natural domain of P_2 (Delta^{1/6} x 1) P_2, so numerical test families built from symmetrised products sample the wrong subspace.

traps.text: Measure the vanishing orders on the shifted diagonals numerically using S-symmetrised product test vectors.
traps.why: Such vectors lie outside D_nat, so the sampling would measure the wrong subspace.

steps: The effective one-spectator multiplier of P_n (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x ... x 1) P_n is g(u) = S(u) S(i pi/3 - u), studied on the strip -pi/3 < Im u < 0 for Bullough-Dodd S at B = 1/2.
At u = -i pi/6, S(u) has a simple pole while S(i pi/3 - u) = S(i pi/2) is a double zero of S, so g has a simple zero at u = -i pi/6.
At u = 0, S(i pi/3 - u) meets the fusion pole of S at i pi/3 while S(0) = -1, so g has a simple pole on the boundary Im u = 0 with residue Res_{i pi/3} S.
At u = -i pi/3, S(u) has a simple zero while S(i pi/3 - u) = S(2 i pi/3) has a simple pole, so g is regular at that boundary point.
Hence f_k(zeta) = prod_{j<k} g(zeta - theta_j) has k - 1 simple Blaschke zeros at theta_j - i pi/6 and k - 1 simple boundary poles at the real points theta_j.

traps.text: Read the n - 1 Blaschke zeros of f_n as a deficiency count, giving indices (1, 0) and no self-adjoint extension at n = 2.
traps.why: This contradicts Tanimoto Prop 4.7 at n = 2; Theorem 4.1 of 1508 does not apply to this multiplier.

traps.text: Identify the Blaschke zeros of f_n with the prescribed zeros of natural-domain vectors, since both number one per spectator.
traps.why: They sit at different depths, pi/6 versus pi/3, from different singularities of S; the equal count is a coincidence.

steps: In a boost band N - 1 < t_1 + t_2 <= N, let Phi_1, Phi_2 be L^2 with exp(pi t_1/6) Phi_1 + exp(pi t_2/6) Phi_2 in L^2; ask whether exp(pi t_1/6) Phi_1 is in L^2.
Every point of the band N - 1 < t_1 + t_2 <= N satisfies min(t_1, t_2) <= N/2, so the band is covered by the regions {t_1 <= N/2} and {t_2 <= N/2}.
On the region {t_2 <= N/2}, exp(pi t_2/6) is bounded by exp(pi N/12), so exp(pi t_2/6) Phi_2 is in L^2 on that region.
On {t_2 <= N/2}, exp(pi t_1/6) Phi_1 equals the L^2 sum minus the L^2 function exp(pi t_2/6) Phi_2, hence is in L^2 on that region.
On {t_1 <= N/2}, exp(pi t_1/6) is bounded by exp(pi N/12), so exp(pi t_1/6) Phi_1 is in L^2 on that region as well.
Therefore exp(pi t_1/6) Phi_1 is in L^2 on the whole band; this two-term pigeonhole is Tanimoto's Lemma 4.6 behind his n = 2 result for P_2 (Delta^{1/6} x 1) P_2.

traps.text: Run the same pigeonhole with three terms, using min(t_1, t_2, t_3) <= N/3 in the band N - 1 < t_1 + t_2 + t_3 <= N.
traps.why: With three terms two can cancel at arbitrarily large t_k inside one band (Proposition D7); the scalar statement is false.

steps: Question: for n = 3, do L^2 functions Phi_1, Phi_2, Phi_3 on the band -1 < t_1 + t_2 + t_3 <= 0 with sum_k exp(a t_k) Phi_k in L^2, a = pi/6, force exp(a t_1) Phi_1 in L^2?
For T > 0 the cube B_T of side 1/4 centred at (T, T, -2T - 1/2) has coordinate sum in (-7/8, -1/8), so B_T lies inside the band.
Set Phi_1 = indicator of B_T, Phi_2 = -exp(a(t_1 - t_2)) times indicator of B_T, Phi_3 = 0; Phi_2 has L^2 norm bounded uniformly in T since t_1 - t_2 is bounded on B_T.
Then exp(a t_1) Phi_1 + exp(a t_2) Phi_2 = exp(a t_1) - exp(a t_1) = 0 pointwise on B_T, so the three-term sum is in L^2 with norm zero.
Yet ||exp(a t_1) Phi_1|| >= (1/4)^{3/2} exp(a(T - 1/8)) for the indicator Phi_1 of B_T, which tends to infinity as T grows.
So the scalar band lemma fails for n = 3; a proof for P_3 (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x 1) P_3 must use the correlation Phi_k = W_k Phi through the S-dressed unitaries.

traps.text: Bound exp(a t_1) Phi_1 by pigeonholing min(t_k) <= N/3 and subtracting the other two terms, as in the two-particle case.
traps.why: The sum does not control any single term: two terms can cancel pointwise at large t_1 = t_2 = T.

steps: The free (S = 1) part of the n = 3 fibre operator of 3 P_3 (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x 1) P_3 is the Fourier multiplier sigma_0(p, q) = e^{-pi p/3} + e^{pi (p - q)/3} + e^{pi q/3}.
The three exponents -pi p/3, pi (p - q)/3 and pi q/3 sum to zero, so the product of the three positive terms of sigma_0(p, q) equals 1.
By AM-GM, sigma_0(p, q) >= 3 times the cube root of that product, i.e. sigma_0 >= 3, with equality only when all three terms equal 1, at p = q = 0.
So sigma_0 is real, positive and zero-free, and multiplication by sigma_0(p, q) is a self-adjoint operator with spectrum contained in [3, infinity).
Symmetrisation reduces the Weyl-group-invariant free operator, so the S = 1 control 3 Sym (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x 1) Sym is self-adjoint with spectrum in [3, infinity).

traps.text: Conclude that with the true S the fibre operator 3 P_3 (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x 1) P_3 also has spectrum in [3, infinity).
traps.why: The S-dressing lowers the bottom: the true-S Galerkin minimum is 2.889 < 3; only positivity of the operator is exact.

steps: T^chi_n = n P_n (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x ... x 1) P_n, where Delta^{1/6} continues theta_1 -> theta_1 - i pi/3 and P_n is the S-symmetriser built from S-factors of rapidity differences.

Delta^{1/6} x 1 x ... x 1 is a Fourier multiplier commuting with real translations, and P_n commutes with the total boost Psi(t) -> Psi(t - s(1,...,1)) because its S-factors depend only on differences.
Hence T^chi_n commutes with the total boost and decomposes over fibres Psi = e^{iK(theta_1 + ... + theta_n)} psi(differences), each fibre of dimension n - 1.
On such a fibre, the shift theta_1 -> theta_1 - i pi/3 multiplies e^{iK(theta_1 + ... + theta_n)} by the positive constant e^{K pi/3} and acts on psi exactly as at K = 0.
So every K-fibre operator of T^chi_n is e^{K pi/3} times the K = 0 fibre operator, and K = 0 is without loss of generality for essential self-adjointness of T^chi_n.

traps.text: Use translation invariance of chi_n(f) with its test-function multipliers to obtain momentum conservation and a centre-of-mass separation.
traps.why: chi is covariant, U chi(f) U^* = chi(f_{a,lambda}); translations move f, so the operator with multipliers commutes with no translation.

traps.text: Use a single-coordinate boost as an additional conserved quantity to reduce the n = 3 fibre operator to one variable.
traps.why: P_n mixes coordinates, so only the total boost commutes; the n = 3 fibre stays two-dimensional.

steps: T^chi_3 = 3 P_3 (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x 1) P_3 on S-symmetric vectors equals 3 X^* X with X = (Delta^{1/12} x 1 x 1) P_3, as in Tanimoto Prop 4.7.
Hence T^chi_3 = 3 P_3 (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x 1) P_3 is a positive symmetric operator, with <Psi, T^chi_3 Psi> >= 0 on its domain.
A semibounded symmetric operator has equal deficiency indices, so n_+ = n_- for T^chi_3 = 3 P_3 (Delta^{1/6} x 1 x 1) P_3.
For the positive symmetric operator T^chi_3, essential self-adjointness is equivalent to density of Ran(T^chi_3 + 1) evaluated on the core.
So the n = 3 question for T^chi_3 is whether the common deficiency index is zero, and equal detector values at T - i and T + i carry no information.

traps.text: Decide the n = 3 case from the sign of a half-line Wiener-Hopf index 1/2, computed as the winding of S divided by 2.
traps.why: No theorem assigns this index; the indices are equal anyway, and the winding is consumed on the facets by the n = 2 problem.

traps.text: Treat the equality sigma_min(T - i) = sigma_min(T + i) in the n = 3 fibre numerics as evidence for essential self-adjointness.
traps.why: The equality is forced by positivity of T^chi_3, since n_+ = n_-.
